Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. The Weekly is the universal subscription rhythm. The brand puts the cadence in the brand position. Plain, modern, immediately legible.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern independent newsletters have become a real publishing category. Substack and similar platforms have created direct relationships between writers and readers. The customer is design-literate and willing to pay a small monthly fee for one or two writers they trust.
Modern.competitorLandscape: The Browser (thebrowser.com) holds the curated-reading peer position. Stratechery (stratechery.com) sits at the analyst-newsletter tier. Lenny's Newsletter (lennysnewsletter.com) does the professional-development middle. We sit closer to The Browser in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: An independent newsletter for the one good read on Sunday morning.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 50. Already pays for two or three newsletters. Reads The Atlantic, The New Yorker, or the equivalent. Wants writing, not 'content'.

dos: Write like a writer, not a content marketer
Show the publishing schedule and the unsubscribe link clearly
Speak to the reader as a reader
donts: Photograph the author against neutral backdrops

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. THE WEEKLY in a tight modern serif, all caps, two words on one line. A small geometric mark, a single thin underline beneath, used as the favicon and in section dividers within the newsletter.

typography.primary: Tiempos Text for the wordmark and body type
typography.secondary: Söhne for headlines and the editor's note
typography.rationale: A classical serif for the reading body. A modern grotesk for the operational signage. The pair feels like an editorial publication, not a content product.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No referral programs. No growth-hacker subject-line testing. No 'mega-thread' content. No celebrity-author marketing.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: An email that arrives at 8 a.m. Sunday. A simple web archive. A monthly podcast recorded by the author, in long form, no edits. No social media presence beyond a single archive.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words. Despatch is the older British spelling of dispatch, the heritage word for a letter from a war correspondent or a foreign attaché. The definite article makes it an institution. The whole name reads as a heritage publication with a quiet, long-running editorial voice.
Luxury.story: The Despatch was founded by a single editor who had spent decades inside major publications and wanted to write to a smaller, more careful set of readers. The newsletter accepts a limited number of subscribers each year. Some subscribers have been with the publication since it opened.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end independent publishing has been moving toward larger Substack operations and bigger marketing. There's a parallel market for small heritage publications in the older editorial tradition. Few readers, long-form essays, decades-long subscriptions.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Harper's Magazine (harpers.org) holds the institutional heritage peer. The Paris Review (theparisreview.org) sits at the literary tier. The Browser (thebrowser.com) does the modern curated-reading middle. We sit smaller and quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small heritage publication with a limited subscription and a long editorial calendar.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy, often inherited. Reads The Atlantic, The New Yorker, Harper's. Pays for a small number of cultural subscriptions. Values the editor's voice.

dos: Write long-form essays without web-style headlines
Send a paper supplement once a year

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn pen-nib hallmark, used on the email masthead, the printed annual supplement, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and printed material
typography.secondary: Söhne for the email operational surfaces
typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the editorial tone. A modern grotesk handles the few operational surfaces.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No referral programs. No social media presence. No content-marketing strategy. No celebrity-author marketing.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Letter is the oldest, plainest word for what a newsletter actually is. The brand sits on the form itself, before the platform, the subject line, and the growth metric.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most independent publications have elaborate names, brand worlds, and origin stories. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the form: a letter, sent weekly, read at leisure.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most newsletters fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some early Substack one-author publications and the no-name aesthetic of certain mailing-list traditions.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A weekly letter. No branded archive, no welcome series, no growth strategy.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who already read two newsletters a week. They want a third that's plainer than the rest. They will not click a referral link.

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. LETTER in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, six letters with generous space. No icon. The email masthead, the web archive, and the unsubscribe page all carry the wordmark and nothing else.

typography.rationale: One face. The email, the archive, and the unsubscribe page all carry the same wordmark.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No referral program. No welcome series. No growth-hacker subject lines. No social media presence.

Corporate.tagline: Editorial newsletter services for the enterprise.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Editor is the role at the center of every good newsletter. & Co. closes it as a small services firm. The pair sits on the editorial discipline at the heart of the work, not the platform or the technology around it.
Corporate.industrySummary: Branded newsletters for enterprise clients is a real B2B category. Companies want their own editorial newsletter operations: brand-led publications that build owned audiences. The category is mostly served by content marketing agencies and a few specialists.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Stripe Press (press.stripe.com) holds the brand-publishing peer position at the giant tier. Industry Audio (industryaudio.com) does the branded-audio adjacent middle. Foreword (forewordmedia.co) sits in the modern peer. We sit smaller and more focused on the enterprise editorial side.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Editorial newsletter operations for enterprise brands that take owned audiences seriously.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Enterprise brands want editorial newsletter operations with the discipline of a real publication. The category incumbents are content marketers. We position on editorial depth and brand discipline.

targetAudience.primary: Chief Brand Officers, VPs of Content, and Heads of Audience Development at enterprise companies. They sign multi-year editorial-services contracts.
motivations: Reporting on owned-audience growth and retention
Single partner across editorial, design, and distribution

dos: Show case studies with audience retention data
Speak to the brand and content leader together
donts: Promote individual newsletters on consumer social

messagingPillars.name: Editorial discipline
messagingPillars.description: Newsletters built like real publications, with editors, calendars, and standards.

messagingPillars.name: Owned audience growth
messagingPillars.description: Audience growth measured against retention and engagement, not just subscriber counts.

messagingPillars.name: One partner across editorial and operations
messagingPillars.description: Strategy, editorial, design, distribution, and reporting under one engagement.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small hand-drawn ampersand becoming the firm's hallmark. The mark appears on letterhead, the masthead of each client newsletter, and the wax seal of every printed engagement letter.

typography.primary: Inter for marketing and B2B materials
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed quarterly reports
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital. The serif handles formal quarterly business reviews and printed editorial portfolios.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No D2C newsletter under our own brand. No celebrity-author partnerships. No content-marketing-by-the-page services. The firm sells through enterprise editorial procurement.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Open Rate is the newsletter-industry metric that every publisher obsesses over and most publishers misrepresent. The brand names the universal anxiety. Loud, self-aware, and immediately legible to anyone who has ever sent an email blast.
Creative.manifesto: Most newsletter brands sell growth, audience, and reach. We made Open Rate because the actual experience of running a newsletter is watching the open rate slip from 40% to 22%, then to 14%, then wondering whether anyone reads any of it. The brand is honest about the work. We are for the writers who keep sending anyway.
Creative.industrySummary: Newsletter branding has been polished, growth-focused, and slightly anxious. There's room for a brand that's warm, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and serious about the actual quiet work of writing for a small loyal audience.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Substack (substack.com) holds the platform peer position. Beehiiv (beehiiv.com) sits in the modern platform tier. Buttondown (buttondown.com) does the small-publisher middle. We are not a platform; we are a brand for the writers on those platforms.
Creative.positioningStatement: A small publication brand for writers who keep sending the newsletter anyway.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 50. Already runs a small newsletter or wants to. Has watched the open rate slip. Wants a brand that sees them rather than sells them growth tactics.

dos: Make jokes about the open rate
Quote real subject lines that worked
Talk like the writer who has the dashboard open
donts: Photograph models reading newsletters on phones

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy display serif with the O of OPEN stylized as a small envelope opening. Standalone envelope-O icon for stickers, social profiles, and the back of every welcome email.

colorPalette.name: Inbox Red
colorPalette.usage: Primary brand color, hero surfaces, stickers

typography.primary: Migra for the wordmark and big display
typography.secondary: PP Neue Montreal for body and email examples
typography.rationale: Migra has warmth. Neue Montreal handles the readable bits. The pair feels designed and a little defiant.

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not a platform. Not a growth-hacker tool. Not afraid of red. Not too cool to admit the open rate is hard.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A weekly newsletter that's mostly funny subject lines from the community. Stickers in every welcome envelope. A small annual meetup for newsletter writers. A merch line of two tees that say OPEN RATE across the back.
